clue.text: Fast and safe

definitions.meaning: fast as in firmly fixed, held tight
safe as in protected from danger

explanation.definitionFit: Both senses share the idea of being firmly fastened and protected: a door made fast is locked, and a protected place is out of harm's way.

clue.text: Walks like a Lord-rather than burglars removing their loot?

definitions.meaning: struts arrogantly, as a lord might
read as those who carry off swag, a burglar's stolen goods

explanation.definitionFit: The verb means strutting with arrogance; split as swag-gers it names those who make off with swag, a thief's plunder.

clue.text: Military man sounds a bit of a nut

indicators.note: sounds signals that the word is pronounced like the inner part of a nut

parts.note: the kernel is the edible part inside a nut

explanation.surface: Calling an army officer slightly crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit of a nut' suggests mildly mad; it is the kernel, which is pronounced the same as the officer's rank.
explanation.definitionFit: This senior army officer ranks above a major.

clue.text: Official gets point right in the back

indicators.note: the point and right go in the word for the back

parts.note: the rear is the back
the gist is the main point

explanation.surface: An officer who gets stabbed in the back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point' looks like a blade and 'in the back' like a stabbing; 'in' is the container signal and 'the back' supplies the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: This official keeps records, such as births, marriages and deaths.

clue.text: From Lincoln a road even further North

parts.note: Abraham Lincoln is familiarly Abe
e'en is the poetic contraction of even

explanation.surface: Directions for a motorist heading north from the cathedral city of Lincoln up an old road.
explanation.walkthrough: Lincoln is not the English city but the US president, Abe. 'Even' gives the poetic E'EN. The definition is relative: this Scottish city lies further north than Lincoln.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish granite city sits on the north-east coast, far to the north of Lincoln in England.

clue.text: Footballers take in a golf club by a form of remote control

parts.note: backs are defensive football players
to take in food is to eat
a driver is a golf club

explanation.surface: Football players bring along a golf club.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is playful: a passenger who directs the driver from behind is controlling the car remotely.
explanation.definitionFit: A passenger who gives unwanted directions controls the car from the back seat, at a distance.

clue.text: Herb of grace, including by divine grace a Dickensian type

indicators.note: the herb takes the abbreviation inside it

parts.note: rue is traditionally called the herb of grace
DG stands for Dei gratia, Latin for by the grace of God, as on British coins

explanation.surface: A herb with a sacred character, likened to a figure from Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnaby Rudge is the title character of a Dickens novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Barnaby, title hero of a Dickens novel, bears this surname, so he is a character from that author's works.

clue.text: Prohibition would seize me up, love

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the words seize me are read from bottom to top

parts.note: to seize is to grab
taken as written
love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: A ban that would make someone grab their sweetheart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses GRAB ME to EMBARG, then love adds O.
explanation.definitionFit: A ban on trade is an official prohibition.

clue.text: Not a railway official

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Denying that someone works on the railways.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as 'not a railway official'; the definition is just 'official'.
explanation.definitionFit: This legal official certifies documents and witnesses signatures.

clue.text: Dusty's income makes us still more tight

indicators.note: makes means the letters of still more tight are formed into something new

explanation.surface: Someone's earnings force us to be even more stingy.
explanation.walkthrough: Anyone surnamed Miller is nicknamed 'Dusty' in Britain, so Dusty's income is what feeds a miller's mill.
explanation.definitionFit: A miller's income comes from corn to grind, and the idiom means anything that brings profit or advantage.

clue.text: Real logic can be expressed in symbolic terms

indicators.note: the letters of the words real logic are expressed, that is squeezed out and reshaped, into a new order

explanation.surface: A philosopher's claim that reasoning can be written down in formal notation.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests symbolic logic; in fact 'expressed' tells you to rearrange REAL LOGIC.
explanation.definitionFit: An allegory conveys its meaning through symbols, so a story told in symbolic terms is allegorical.

clue.text: Come out with it, girl !

parts.note: reads like urging a girl to speak her mind, but a ... 'comes out' into society at her first ball

explanation.surface: Someone impatiently urging a young woman to say what she means.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come out with it' sounds like 'speak up', but a debutante's coming out is her first formal appearance in society.
explanation.definitionFit: A first public appearance, like a society girl's coming-out ball, is a first showing or launch.

clue.text: A creation of Epstein's

parts.note: the sculptor Jacob Epstein carved a famous marble pregnant figure named after the first book of the Bible, a word that itself means creation

explanation.surface: A work by the sculptor Jacob Epstein.
explanation.walkthrough: Two readings in one: the word means 'a creation' or origin, and it is also the title of Jacob Epstein's 1930s marble sculpture of a pregnant woman.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means origin or coming into being, and is also the title of Epstein's famous statue.

clue.text: Direction to auditor — working in a clip-joint ?

parts.note: S, for south, is a compass direction
an auditor is literally a hearer or listener

explanation.surface: An instruction to a listener about someone employed in a shady nightclub.
explanation.walkthrough: A clip-joint is slang for a club that overcharges, but here it is a sheep-shearing shed where fleeces are clipped.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who clips sheep for their wool works in a shed where clipping goes on.

clue.text: Boss used to draw the line

definitions.meaning: a boss is one who governs or commands
a straight-edged strip used for drawing straight lines

explanation.definitionFit: One word covers a sovereign who governs and the measuring strip with which one draws straight lines.

clue.text: It goes the rounds in China, sometimes full of medicine

definitions.text: It goes the rounds in China, sometimes full of medicine

parts.words: It goes the rounds in China, sometimes full of medicine
parts.note: reads like something travelling round the country of China, but it stirs round a china cup and measures out doses of medicine

explanation.surface: Something that tours China and sometimes carries medicines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' is capitalised to suggest the country; it is the crockery in which tea is stirred round and round. Doses of medicine are measured by the spoonful.
explanation.definitionFit: A small spoon stirs tea in a china cup and is the standard household measure for a dose of medicine.

clue.text: A roundabout way to size up a fairy ?

parts.note: a peri is a fairy in Persian myth
a meter is a device used to size things up

explanation.surface: An indirect way of assessing a fairy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roundabout' looks like indirect, but means going round: the way round the edge.
explanation.definitionFit: The boundary around an area is the way round it.

clue.text: Campaigner for equality takes a measure in the bar

indicators.note: the measure goes in the word for the bar

parts.note: a lever is a bar used to prise
an ell is an old measure of length

explanation.surface: An activist takes a drink in the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Measure' and 'bar' suggest a pub drink; they are ELL, an old cloth length, and LEVER. The Levellers were 17th-century English radicals.
explanation.definitionFit: The Levellers of the English Civil War campaigned for equal rights; the word names anyone seeking to level society.

clue.text: What music did in Shelley's memory

definitions.text: What music did in Shelley's memory

parts.words: What music did in Shelley's memory
parts.note: alludes to Shelley's poem that begins 'Music, when soft voices die' and says the music lingers on in the memory

explanation.surface: A question about the music that Shelley remembered.
explanation.walkthrough: Shelley's lines 'Music, when soft voices die, / Vibrates in the memory' supply the verb, put into the past tense.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet wrote that music trembles on in the memory; the past tense of that quivering verb fits the clue.

clue.text: Dangerous sea calf

parts.note: reads like a young seal or whale, but a glacier 'calves' great blocks of floating ice into the sea

explanation.surface: A warning about a young sea creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calf' suggests a baby seal; it is a block calved from a glacier, a hazard to shipping.
explanation.definitionFit: A mass of floating ice broken from a glacier is called a calf, and it endangers ships.

clue.text: Evil root of India ?

parts.note: money is the root of all evil, so the evil root in India is that country's currency unit

explanation.surface: A question about the source of wickedness in India.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'money is the root of all evil' turns 'evil root' into money, and India's money is its currency unit.
explanation.definitionFit: The basic currency unit of India is a form of money, which the proverb calls the root of all evil.

clue.text: Alarmed at a small cut in salary

indicators.note: the small cut goes in the word for salary

parts.note: pay is salary
a nick is a small cut

explanation.surface: Distressed at a modest reduction in wages.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a wage reduction; 'in' is the container signal, so the small cut goes inside the salary word rather than reducing it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone panicky is frightened and agitated.

clue.text: Chap gets leg broken in a laundry

parts.note: a chap is a man

indicators.note: broken means the letters of leg are smashed and reassembled

explanation.surface: A man breaks his leg in an accident at the laundry.
explanation.definitionFit: A wringer with rollers for squeezing water from washed clothes was standard equipment in a laundry.

clue.text: Act I — Outside Oriental Compound

indicators.note: the words act I sit outside the letter for oriental, wrapping round it

parts.note: Act I is read as act one
E, for east, is the oriental direction

explanation.surface: A stage direction for the opening act, set outside some eastern enclosure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Compound' looks like an enclosure for the scene; it is a chemical compound, the solvent in nail-varnish remover.
explanation.definitionFit: This volatile solvent is a chemical compound of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

clue.text: Arrange Society class

definitions.meaning: to arrange is to put in sequence
a society such as a religious brotherhood of monks
a class or rank, as in a taxonomic grouping

explanation.definitionFit: One word means to arrange things, a brotherhood like the Jesuits, and a rank or category in biology.

clue.text: Huge fellows in semi-disarray

indicators.note: the word for fellows goes in the middle of the jumbled letters
disarray means the letters of semi are thrown into disorder

parts.note: fellows are men

explanation.surface: Large men in a state of partial untidiness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disarray' rearranges SEMI into IMSE, with MEN placed in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something of vast size.

clue.text: Concurred decapitation needed for this vice

indicators.note: decapitation means the head, the first letter, is cut off the word

parts.note: concurred means agreed

explanation.surface: A remark that beheading is the punishment this sin requires.
explanation.walkthrough: AGREED loses its head, its first letter A.
explanation.definitionFit: Avarice, one of the seven deadly sins, is a classic example of a vice.

clue.text: I make an impression on one State, just the same

parts.note: a dent is an impression left in a surface
I is the Roman numeral one
CAL is an abbreviation for California, a US state

explanation.surface: A boast of making a mark on a particular state, followed by the shrug that it is all the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that are exactly alike are just the same as each other.

clue.text: Puck's mundane 40-minute job to do so

definitions.text: Puck's mundane 40-minute job to do so

parts.words: Puck's mundane 40-minute job to do so
parts.note: in A Midsummer Night's Dream Puck promises to put a girdle round about the earth in forty minutes; mundane here means of the world

explanation.surface: Something dull that Puck took forty minutes to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mundane' looks like 'boring' but means 'worldly': Puck boasts 'I'll put a girdle round about the earth in forty minutes', which is the verb's meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: To encircle with a belt is what Puck did when he girdled the globe.

clue.text: It is commonly booked in church

definitions.text: It is commonly booked in church

parts.words: It is commonly booked in church
parts.note: booked suggests a reservation, but in an Anglican church these words are set down in the Book of Common ...

explanation.surface: Something people often reserve at a church, like a wedding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commonly booked' hints at the Book of Common Prayer, the Church of England's service book.
explanation.definitionFit: A petition to God is set out in the church's service book, the Book of Common Prayer.
